subject: calculus
subtopics: the local (relative) maximum and minimum, defined on a neighbourhood
the global (absolute) maximum and minimum on a stated domain
Fermat's theorem: an interior local extremum of a differentiable function forces f' = 0, and why the converse fails
stationary points (f' = 0) against critical points (f' = 0 or f' undefined)
the first-derivative (sign) test and the multiplicity of a zero of f'
the second-derivative test, including the inconclusive case f'' = 0
the higher-derivative test: the order of the first non-vanishing derivative
the extreme value theorem and the closed-interval candidate list of critical points plus endpoints
monotonicity: the sign of f' on an interval, and the union-of-intervals trap
extrema of piecewise and absolute-value functions, and at points where f' does not exist
local extrema at the endpoints of the domain, and the definitional disagreement
counting the extrema of a cubic (b^2 against 3ac) and of a quartic
extrema of trigonometric functions on a restricted interval
stationary points of a function of two variables and the rt - s^2 test
setting up an optimisation word problem and choosing the interval

chosen.title: 18.01 Single Variable Calculus, Lecture 12 (Fall 2007): maxima and minima
chosen.note: the full lecture transcript was read from its opening to the related-rates hand-off; the wire-into-two-squares worked example and the warning about unchecked endpoints are quoted from it, the OCW lecture 11 page being the course index entry
covers: the max-min procedure on a word problem: draw, name the variables, write the objective, then differentiate
the wire of length 1 cut into two squares, with A(x) = x^2/16 + (1-x)^2/16, critical point x = 1/2 and value 1/32
the explicit warning that the critical point gave the least area while the largest area sits at the ends of the interval
the distinction between the minimum value, the minimum point and the critical point
the standing instruction to check the end points after the critical points
chosen.why: The one source this run whose lecture could be read end to end. It is not GATE material, but it supplies the two ideas the GATE questions actually test - the closed-interval candidate list and the fact that a stationary point may be the opposite of the extremum asked for - in the lecturer's own words, and its worked example is verified here independently (1/32 at x = 1/2, 1/16 in the limit). Read in full from the transcript of 18.01 Lecture 12.

chosen.title: Maxima & Minima (13 min), Engineering Mathematics for GATE
chosen.note: Hindi-medium lecture; the platform's published English AI chapter summary with timestamps was read in full, the lecture itself was not. Chapters used: 0:00-2:00 local and global extrema drawn on [a,b], 2:00-5:00 the three statements S1/S2/S3, 5:00-10:00 the x^3 saddle point and the cusp maximum, 10:00-13:20 the closed-interval algorithm
covers: local and global extrema drawn on a closed interval [a, b] with the points m1..m5 (0:00-2:00)
the three statements S1 (at every maximum/minimum f' = 0), S2 (if f' = 0 then an extremum) and S3, with x^3 as the counterexample to S2 (2:00-10:00)
a sharp corner at a maximum, where f' does not exist, as the counterexample to 'f' = 0 is necessary' (5:00-10:00)
the closed-interval algorithm: check where f'(x) = 0, check the endpoints f(a) and f(b), and check points where f' is undefined (10:00-13:20)
chosen.why: The only GATE-oriented teaching of this topic that could be read this run, and its order is the order of the cards: definitions, then the two false converses, then the algorithm. It is a Hindi-medium lecture and what was readable is the platform's published English AI chapter summary with timestamps, so the cards use its structure and its counterexamples and quote no sentence of the lecturer.

chosen.title: 26 Jan - EM - Calculus Part 2, the maxima and minima segment
chosen.note: Hindi-medium live class; the English AI chapter summary was read for the stationary-versus-critical distinction (2:00-5:00) and the second-derivative test with its inconclusive case (5:00-15:00)
covers: the definition of a stationary point as f'(a) = 0 with a horizontal tangent, and of a critical point as f'(a) = 0 or f'(a) undefined (2:00-5:00)
the second-derivative test with the rule f'' > 0 minimum, f'' < 0 maximum, and the explicit statement that f'' = 0 is inconclusive and needs higher derivatives (5:00-15:00)
worked examples f(x) = x, x^2, x^3 and x^3/3 - x, the last with a maximum at -1 and a minimum at 1 (10:00-15:00)
chosen.why: Used for exactly the two things the 13-minute lesson does not cover: the stationary/critical distinction and the second-derivative test with its inconclusive case. Same channel as the lesson above and the same access limit (Hindi-medium, English AI summary), recorded separately because it is a different recording with different content.

chosen.title: Calculus I, section 4.3: Minimum and Maximum Values
chosen.channel: Paul's Online Math Notes, Lamar University
chosen.note: read in full: the four definitions, the statement that relative extrema are usually taken to be interior with an explicit note that some authors disagree, Fermat's theorem and the |x| counterexample to its converse
covers: the four definitions of absolute and relative maximum and minimum
the statement that relative extrema are usually taken to occur only at interior points, with an explicit note that some authors disagree - the disagreement GATE CSE 2012 Q.9 runs into
Fermat's theorem and the |x| counterexample showing that extrema also occur where f' does not exist
the critical-point vocabulary and the extreme value theorem
chosen.why: Chosen for correctness and for beginner accessibility rather than exam framing: it is the readable English source that states every definition and hypothesis the cards depend on, including the endpoint convention as a disagreement rather than a fact. Read in full.

notes: The syllabus names the topic in three words, so the fifteen subtopics above are this run's enumeration from the standard treatment (Stewart 4.1-4.3, NCERT chapter 6, Paul's notes) and from the six verified CSE questions, not a quotation from the syllabus.

This run read one lecture transcript end to end (MIT 18.01 Lecture 12), which the previous topic could not do. YouTube itself still served no caption track, so no YouTube lecture is quoted; the two GATE-oriented lectures used are recorded from the platform's published English AI chapter summaries of Hindi-medium classes and are marked translated.

The non-English material is Hindi-medium throughout (two Knowledge Gate recordings) and reaches the cards only through English AI summaries, so the translation sits two layers from the lecture; no card quotes a Hindi sentence.
GATE CSE 2015 Set 2 GA-3 (maximum of 1 - |x|) is a General Aptitude question and is excluded from the PYQ set for that reason; it is still a fair practice question and appears nowhere as a PYQ.
GATE CSE 1998's descriptive maxima question is excluded by the repository's MCQ/MSQ/NAT-only schema and is named as a gap.

Every PYQ in this topic is SOURCED against a GATE Overflow accepted answer rather than key-verified against an official answer key, and no marks field is recorded, because no official paper or key was fetched this run.
